analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and requires warrants before the government spies on Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or a single cosponsor in the House and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), the law governing government surveillance for intelligence purposes. In its place, it would require federal officers to get an ordinary criminal warrant before electronically surveilling a U.S. citizen, physically searching their property, compelling their phone or business records, or targeting them for intelligence collection. It would also bar evidence gathered under a presidential intelligence directive or by surveilling someone else from being used against a U.S. citizen in any proceeding, and it would make willful violations a crime punishable by at least five years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, whose phone records, emails, homes, and business records could no longer be collected or searched for intelligence purposes without a warrant issued by a regular federal court. Anyone whose information was swept up during surveillance of a foreign target could no longer have that information used against them in court. It also protects the privacy of every citizen from warrantless intelligence collection, whether they are under investigation or not.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Any American whose communications or records could be swept up

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the entire FISA chapter of federal law, repealing the authorities that allow electronic surveillance and access to business records for foreign intelligence purposes without a regular court order.

Requires a federal judge to issue a warrant before a government officer conducts electronic surveillance of a U.S. citizen, physically searches property under their exclusive control, obtains their records, or targets them to acquire foreign intelligence.

Bars information about a U.S. citizen gathered under Executive Order 12333 or during surveillance of a non-citizen from being used in evidence or as part of any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding or investigation.

Creates criminal penalties — a fine up to $10,000 or at least five years in prison — for government officers who intentionally conduct these searches without statutory authorization or knowingly use information obtained without it.

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence and law enforcement agencies — the FBI, NSA, and CIA — would lose the streamlined legal authorities FISA provides for gathering foreign intelligence, and would face criminal exposure for violating the new warrant requirements. Supporters of FISA argue this would make it harder to track foreign spies and terrorists and harder to follow the communications of foreign targets that touch U.S. persons.

drawbacks.text: Repealing FISA entirely removes a legal framework that includes court oversight, rather than narrowing it, and would leave no statutory process for intelligence agencies to lawfully monitor foreign powers and agents on U.S. soil, where the previous law's foreign-focused warrant process was designed to apply.

The bill would bar even properly collected foreign intelligence from being used against a U.S. citizen in any proceeding, which critics would say hampers prosecutions of terrorism and espionage cases where the evidence was lawfully gathered while surveilling a foreign target.
The bill's protections apply only to U.S. citizens, leaving the same warrantless surveillance authorities available against non-citizens in the United States, including legal residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains for Americans are real: warrantless access to citizens' records and communications, and the use of presidentially-directed surveillance material against them, would end. The cost is design, not intent: repealing the entire FISA statute rather than amending it removes the court process used to lawfully surveil foreign agents in the United States, which even many FISA critics treat as a problem to be fixed rather than a framework to be scrapped. The lack of any cosponsors suggests members across both parties did not view full repeal as a workable trade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees in May 2020, and neither ever took it up; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on May 12, 2020, two months after Congress had passed an amended reauthorization of core FISA surveillance powers.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence; no further action was ever listed in its history.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill, and it never received a committee hearing or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national security agencies and the surveillance authorities the bill would have repealed kept their powers untouched; the private companies and officials that participate in or rely on FISA surveillance were better off because the bill never advanced. Americans' privacy rights remain subject to the FISA framework the bill sought to eliminate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and the existing FISA framework

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.role: Sponsor, House Freedom Caucus-adjacent conservative from Arizona
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it never drew a cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist to measure support, so the partisan shape of any opposition was never recorded; the bill's sole sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: National security and intelligence agencies (FBI, NSA, CIA)
industries.note: The bill would repeal the legal authorities these agencies use to conduct electronic surveillance and compel records without a regular court warrant, and would expose officers to criminal prosecution for violating it. Their interest in retaining these powers runs against the privacy interest of ordinary citizens in this bill.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and technology companies complying with surveillance orders
industries.note: Firms served as the pipeline for FISA-era pen registers, business records demands, and electronic surveillance; repeal of the framework would end many of those compelled-disclosure obligations, though the bill does not address liability or immunity directly. Their gain or loss is a byproduct of changing the government's collection rules.
